children: Microsoft is limiting its artificial-intelligence models, but it isn't slowing its pace in the AI race.

As investors sent many AI-related stocks lower following calls for a slowdown in AI development, Microsoft on Monday released a draft of a new code of conduct for how it trains and operates its models. The company said there will be limits on its models, including not being able to fulfill requests related to weapons manufacturing or to create violent content, but it didn't explicitly say it would curb growth.

"Superintelligence is the most consequential technology of our time. It will reach far beyond the scope of any one company, shaping the lives and experiences of humanity for generations to come," Microsoft wrote. "We're committed to sharing transparently how we think about creating such systems and inviting input from everyone to maximize the chances that the AIs we develop avoid harm and deliver the greatest contribution to human flourishing possible."
CEO Satya Nadella on Sunday posted to social-media platform X that AI must be focused on "helping humanity and under human control."
If those aren't the principles, then "it's not worth pursuing," Nadella added.
Microsoft's code of conduct stipulated that AI shouldn't exceed human control and that safety and control must be part of the models.
The company added Microsoft AI models won't "assist or perform actions that could result in the clear real-world harms" and that users won't be able to override safety constraints.

"Maintaining human control in an age of superintelligence is at the heart of Humanist AI. That means AI should be defined as much by what it cannot do as what it can. Limits and boundaries, i.e., containment mechanisms, are essential," Microsoft wrote.

Microsoft has bet big on its cloud platform, Azure, and its AI assistant tool CoPilot. The company's capital spending reached $41 billion in the fiscal fourth quarter and $145 billion for the year. Wall Street thinks investors should brace themselves for heavier AI spending in fiscal 2027.

There's not much of an incentive to slow down on what has become Microsoft's major growth engine. The company, however, seemed comfortable setting limits on its models as the conversation and sentiment around AI has shifted toward security risks and exponential threats to humanity.

The timing of Microsoft's public code of conduct release was tied to calls from Elon Musk, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, and Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei to slow down the pace at which AI is developing, citing concerns about cybersecurity and the possibility that humans will lose control of the machine systems.

Investors responded to the warnings on Monday by dumping many highflying AI stocks. Intel and Advanced Micro Devices fell 6.4% and 6%, respectively. Marvell Technology stock also declined 7.6% while Micron Technology dropped 6.2%. Lam Research fell 6.9%, with hardware makers Hewlett Packard Enterprise and Dell Technologies falling 11% and 7%, respectively.
Among optical networking stocks, Corning stock fell 12%, Ciena declined 6.7%, Coherent dropped 11%, and Lumentum moved 8.8% lower.
Microsoft stock, however, wasn't in the red on Monday. Shares advanced 1% to $500.88. Fellow Magnificent Seven stocks Alphabet, Meta Platforms rose 2% and 0.9%, respectively.
Microsoft wasn't backing away from the AI path it's forged, but the company admitted that AI needs guardrails. It's the middle ground and investors approved.
